bib.title: Are NLP Models really able to Solve Simple Math Word Problems?

question: Do NLP math word problem solvers actually solve one-unknown arithmetic MWPs, or do they exploit shallow heuristics in the benchmark datasets?
hypothesis: Existing solvers rely on shallow heuristics (patterns in the story, specific words) rather than reading the question and reasoning.
contributions: We show that the majority of problems in benchmark datasets can be solved by shallow heuristics lacking word-order information or lacking question text.
We create a challenge set called SVAMP for more robust evaluation of methods developed to solve elementary level math word problems.

method.summary: Trains three pre-LLM solvers (Seq2Seq, GTS, Graph2Tree) on MAWPS and ASDiv-A, tests them with the question removed and with a word-order-free constrained model, then builds SVAMP (1000 hand-made variations of 100 ASDiv-A seed problems) and evaluates the same solvers on it. No LLMs or prompting.
method.task: one-unknown arithmetic math word problem to equation (execution accuracy)

datasets.name: MAWPS
datasets.split: 5-fold cross-validation, pre-assigned splits of equal test size

datasets.name: ASDiv-A
datasets.size: 1218 MWPs (arithmetic subset of ASDiv, mostly up to grade 4)

datasets.name: SVAMP
datasets.size: 1000 problems (1098 created, 98 with more than two operators discarded)
datasets.split: evaluation after training on MAWPS+ASDiv-A; also 5-fold CV over seed-example groups when trained with SVAMP
datasets.source: built by authors and colleagues from 100 seed ASDiv-A examples; github.com/arkilpatel/SVAMP
datasets.preprocessing: Seeds: drop types with <20 examples (TVQ-Change, TVQ-Initial, Ceil-Division, Floor-Division) and Difference type; drop examples >40 words; keep single-operator problems; K-Means on RoBERTa sentence embeddings per type, take example nearest centroid; 28 add, 33 sub, 19 mul, 20 div. Checked by an external volunteer for grammar and logic.

models.name: Seq2Seq
models.architecture: BiLSTM encoder, LSTM decoder with attention (Luong 2015)

models.name: GTS
models.architecture: LSTM encoder, tree-based decoder (Xie and Sun 2019)

models.name: Graph2Tree
models.architecture: graph encoder, tree decoder (Zhang et al. 2020)

models.name: Constrained model (FFN + LSTM decoder)
models.architecture: Seq2Seq with LSTM encoder replaced by feed-forward network; decoder starts from average of hidden representations, attends over token states; no word-order information
models.init_from: scratch or non-contextual RoBERTa embedding matrix

training.lr: searched: Seq2Seq S [5e-4,8e-4,1e-3], R [1e-4,2e-4,5e-4]; GTS S [8e-4,1e-3,2e-3], R [5e-4,8e-4,1e-3]; Graph2Tree same as GTS; constrained [1e-3,2e-3]
training.dropout: 0.1 Seq2Seq and constrained; 0.5 GTS and Graph2Tree
training.compute: average time per epoch (s): Seq2Seq 10/40, GTS 60/120, Graph2Tree 60/120, constrained 10/15 (S/R)

limits: Models are 2021 task-specific solvers trained on the data, not prompted LLMs; nothing is shown about LLMs.
Only one-unknown arithmetic MWPs up to grade 4, English; SVAMP has at most two operators and 100 seed problems.
SVAMP made in-house by the authors and colleagues; lower lexical diversity (CLD 0.22 vs 0.50 ASDiv-A).
Authors state they do not claim every model uses specific-word heuristics; only that such a brittle model scores well.
